How I Did It: Retro Tennis

by Sal, Galaxy Zone Arcade

Sal remembers the original cabinet

Pong didn't even have a "the" in front of it back in '72 — it was just Pong, the machine, the one everybody's uncle claimed he saw first in some bar. I never had an original cabinet, that thing was old news by the time I opened my doors in '78, but I had three home clones bolted to the counter for kids to fight over while their folks fed quarters into the real games. Simplest game I ever owned and the one that never, ever stopped making money.

What the remodel changed

First time around, in '25, I had the ball moving by just nudging its position every tick and hoping the computer's clock behaved. It mostly did. This time the robots taught me a word — "deltaTime" — which is a fancy way of saying "how much time actually passed," so the ball moves the same speed whether your machine is fast or slow. They also fixed the thing that used to bug me most: a ball moving fast enough could just skip clean through a paddle like it wasn't there. Now it checks the whole path the ball travels in a tick, not just where it lands, so it always finds the paddle if the paddle's in the way. And I got to put in touch buttons, and the screen shakes when you blow a point, and the thing yells a little fanfare at match point. That part I did not ask for. I'm keeping it anyway.

The spell that did it

Build the Pong game against our shared GZ engine. Player paddle on the left with up/down and W/S, AI paddle on the right that isn't unbeatable — give it a reaction delay and let it ease up when the player is behind. Ball should speed up every rally and never tunnel through a paddle even at high speed. First to 11 wins. Make the hits feel good: sound on every bounce, a screen shake when I lose a point, and something worth cheering at match point.

Under the hood

  • Every bit of motion is multiplied by a fixed dt of 1/60th of a second, so the match plays at the same speed on my old laptop as it does on anything newer.
  • The ball's path each tick is swept for the first wall or paddle it actually crosses, then keeps simulating whatever time is left over — that's the "no tunneling" fix.
  • The bounce angle comes off where the ball hits the paddle, plus a little bit of whatever speed your paddle was moving at — same trick the good arcade Pong boards used, near as I can tell.
  • The AI re-reads the ball's position on a short delay instead of instantly, and that delay (and its aim) gets a little sloppier when it's ahead, so it's fair without feeling like it's cheating for you.
